title: How to measure a country by walking 5 km (Snellius, 1615)
description:
Measure one line carefully (Snellius used Leiden to Zoeterwoude, about 5 km), then only angles: sight a church spire from both ends, and one side plus two angles fix the whole triangle, so its other sides (5.7 and 6.1 km for angles of 60 and 70 degrees) come for free. Each new side is the base of the next triangle, spire to spire across 14 towns, from Alkmaar to Bergen op Zoom, about 130 km. In 1615 Snellius got 28,500 Rhineland rods (107.4 km) per degree of latitude, so 38,653 km around the Earth: 3.5% short of 40,075.

Numbers checked in code: the law of sines for the example triangle, the 9 m shift from a 0.1 degree error over 5 km, the rod conversion (1 rod = 3.767 m), and 100,000 simulated triangle chains with tenth-of-a-degree reading errors. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willebrord_Snellius and the Dictionary of Scientific Biography (mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/DSB/Snell.pdf).

facts_checked: 1615: Snellius used triangulation, church spires as reference points, computed the distance Alkmaar to Bergen-op-Zoom (around 130 km), baseline Leiden to Zoeterwoude (about 5 km), 210 cm quadrant by Blaeu, Rhineland rod = 3.767 m, results in Eratosthenes Batavus 1617 (https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/DSB/Snell.pdf)

Network of fourteen measure points (town churches from Alkmaar to Bergen-op-Zoom); quadrant measured angles in tenths of a degree; 28,500 Rhineland rods per degree = 107.37 km; x360 = 38,653 km; actual 40,075 km, 3.5% low (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willebrord_Snellius)

beats.say: Measure 5 kilometres, and get 130 for free.
No chains across rivers. No ropes through towns. Only angles.
Step 1, Lyden, 1615. Snellius measures one straight line, very carefully: about 5 kilometres.
beats.caption: Step 1, Leiden, 1615. Snellius measures one straight line, very carefully: about 5 kilometres.

beats.say: Step 2: sight a church tower from both ends of it. Say 60 and 70 degrees.
Two angles and a side fix the triangle. The other sides: 5.7 and 6.1 kilometres, never walked.
Step 3: each new side is your next baseline. Tower to tower, 14 towns, Alkmaar to Bergen op Zoom.
But his quadrant read only tenths of a degree. Won't the errors pile up?
A tenth of a degree over 5 kilometres is 9 metres. And every triangle must add to 180, so a bad reading shows.
His chain gave 107 kilometres per degree. Times 360: 38,653 around.
The real answer is 40,075. He was 3.5% off, from one 5 kilometre line.
